- [x] **Enforce migration numbering with a check, not prose.** Raised 2026-09-22 after two in-flight branches both shipped `0069` (`0069_seed_standard_diet.sql` on the diet branch and `0069_assistant_actions.sql` on `claude/assistant-v1-schema`) and both were applied to dev before anyone noticed — the same clash as the two `0067` PRs earlier. CLAUDE.md already says the next number is one past the highest on `main` and that only one in-flight branch may carry a migration, but it is prose that nothing enforces, and `apply-migrations.mjs --status` reports `0 pending` while dev holds rows main has no file for, so the divergence is invisible. Add a check that fails at commit time (`.githooks/pre-commit`) and in CI: a new file under `supabase/migrations/` must be numbered exactly one past the highest on `origin/main`, and no two files may share a number. Worth pairing with a `--drift` mode on `apply-migrations.mjs` that lists rows in `schema_migrations` with no matching file — dev currently has **two**, not three: `--status` reported 72 applied against 70 files on `main` with `0 pending` (checked 2026-09-23), so exactly two recorded rows have no file. They are the two renumberings — `0067_public_resident_cards.sql` (now `0068`) and `0069_assistant_actions.sql` (now `0070`, commit `34bf49e`). `0069_seed_standard_diet.sql` kept its number and is still a file on `main`, so it is not an orphan. Both leftovers are harmless, but note that the count in this item was wrong until someone did the arithmetic by hand — which is the whole argument for the flag: an orphan count nobody can read off a command is an orphan count that drifts in the notes as well as the database.

- [x] **Make production drift visible: nothing records what production has actually run.** Raised 2026-09-22, alongside the numbering item above and arguably the larger half of it. `schema_migrations` lives inside each database, so the repo has no idea what production has applied and `apply-migrations.mjs --status` only ever answers for the database it is pointed at. `0069_seed_standard_diet.sql` was applied to **production** while `main` had no file for it at all, and sat that way until PR #46 merged; dev meanwhile held three rows with no file on `main`, and `--status` cheerfully reported `0 pending` throughout. Drift is silent in both directions and nobody finds out until someone rebuilds a database or renumbers a file. Note the only thing that prevented a second production apply was accidental: `scripts/worktree.mjs new` copies `.env.local` but not `.env.deploy.production`, so a feature worktree physically cannot reach production — while the main checkout has the file and can. That is luck, not design. Worth: a `--drift` mode that diffs `schema_migrations` against the files on `origin/main` for a named environment and names both halves (applied-but-missing, present-but-unapplied); a `--status` that says which files on `origin/main` production has **not** run, so the pre-deploy gap is one command; and a loud refusal (or at least a prompt) when `--env production` is used from a branch whose migration is not yet on `origin/main`, since schema is supposed to reach `main` before any database. See `docs/decisions.md` 2026-09-22 for the 0069 clash this came out of.

- [x] **`deploy.mjs` ships code without ever asking whether the database has the schema it needs.** Raised 2026-09-30 after it went wrong twice in one day. `deploy.mjs` guards a lot before it builds — branch is `main`, working tree clean, `main` level with `origin/main`, `package.json` matching `latestRelease`, `unreleased` empty — and then deploys without checking a single migration. `apply-migrations.mjs --drift <env>` answers exactly that question and already shares its implementation with Settings → System status (`src/lib/migration-drift.ts`), so the work is wiring, not building. **Two consecutive releases, both on 2026-09-30, and the difference between them was luck rather than process:** on `0.10.0` the deploy was started before `0113`–`0116` were applied, and got away with it only because a deploy spends its first minutes building — the migrations were applied alongside it and reached `No drift` at 116 files while the deploy was 134 seconds in and still compiling, so the schema landed before the Worker upload. It was noticed only because an unrelated `--drift` could not write to `deploy.log` (`Device or resource busy`). On `0.10.1` the luck ran out: `0117` went on about an hour *after* the release was live, and its consumer had shipped in that release (`17c7f0d`, the Microchipped tick on `/adopt/[id]`, with `src/app/adopt/[id]/page.tsx` and `src/lib/residents/public.ts` both selecting `is_microchipped`), so the **public adoption profile was querying a column that did not exist**. How long that lasted cannot be established, because that deploy was run without `>> deploy.log` and its start time is unrecorded. Both are written up in `docs/releases/2026-09-30.md`. **What to build:** in the `GUARDED` block (`uat` and `production` only — leave `test` alone, where running ahead is normal and wanted), refuse the deploy when the target database is missing any migration, listing the pending filenames and the `apply-migrations.mjs` command to fix it, and exit `2` like the sibling guards. **Get the comparison right, because the obvious one is wrong:** the rule is *every migration file in the commit being deployed must be applied to the target*, **not** "the target matches `origin/main`". Extra applied rows are fine — schema ahead of code is the safe direction this project deliberately uses, and a migration belonging to the *next* release can legitimately sit on `main` already. `0118` was in exactly that position during `0.10.1`: on `main`, belonging to `#236` which merged after the cut, and correctly not applied. A naive equality check would have refused that deploy for a file it did not need. In practice the two formulations coincide, because the existing guard already requires `HEAD` to equal `origin/main` — but they should not be *written* as the same thing, or the check breaks the first time someone deploys a tag or a hotfix. **And distinguish "the database says it is behind" from "could not ask":** refuse on the first, warn loudly and continue on the second. A deploy already depends on the network, so this is not the `release-prs.mjs` situation where failing closed on a blip was the thing to avoid; but a Supabase timeout should not be able to block a release either. Worth pairing with the reverse check at the other end: `apply-migrations.mjs` could warn when it applies a file whose consumer is not yet deployed, which is the same information read the other way round.

- [x] **Every guard on the deploy is on the copy nobody is served by.** Raised 2026-10-01, and it is the sibling of the item above: that one is now done, which is exactly what makes this one visible. `deploy.mjs` refuses a `uat`/`production` deploy unless the branch is `main`, the tree is clean, `main` is level with `origin/main`, `package.json` matches `latestRelease`, `unreleased` is empty — "ships only a written-down release" — and, since the item above, unless the target database holds every migration the commit carries. **`scripts/pi/deploy-pi.sh` has none of that.** It is 51 lines: `git fetch origin main` → `git checkout main` → `git reset --hard origin/main` → `npm ci` → `npm run build` → `systemctl restart`. It does run `apply-migrations.mjs --status | tail -1`, but only *prints* it, with a comment saying a build against a database missing a migration is still a valid build — which was a reasonable position before `deploy.mjs` started refusing in that exact case, and is now an asymmetry rather than a decision. **And the Pi is the copy that serves users**: `ORIGIN_HOST` is `pi.lannacare.org` in the production block, and `lannacare.org` answers `x-lanna-served-by: pi`. The Worker is the fallback. So the whole release discipline — cut, record, version, schema check — is enforced on the path that answers only when the Pi times out. **What it costs, all three observed rather than theorised:** (a) **code reaches users without a release cut.** Every note in `0.11.0` was already live before it was cut, because the Pi had been reset to `origin/main` by earlier deploys; release notes now describe what people already have, and `/releases` can show an older version than the app's behaviour. (b) **The release-time gate never runs for it.** `docs/release-smoke-test.md`'s "every PR in this release has a completed test plan — check this by hand" is a pre-*deploy* step, and there is no deploy step here to hang it on. (c) **`npx wrangler rollback --env production` is no longer the production rollback.** It reverts the Worker, which is not serving. Rolling the Pi back means `git reset --hard <sha>` and a rebuild, and that is written down nowhere as a rollback path — while four release records in `docs/releases/` state the `wrangler rollback` position as though it were the whole answer. That documentation is wrong from 2026-09-30 onward and should be corrected with this item. **What to build:** the cheap version is to make `deploy-pi.sh` run the same two checks `deploy.mjs` already has, reusing them rather than restating them — `unreleased` empty and `package.json` matching `latestRelease` for a production or uat deploy, and `missingFromDatabase(deployedMigrations(git), applied)` for the schema, refusing with the same messages and keeping "could not ask" a warning. A `--force` for a genuine emergency is fine *if* it prints loudly and the reason ends up in a record; the sign-in outage of 30 September is exactly the case for one, and it was handled properly through a PR anyway. Keep `--env test` unguarded, as `deploy.mjs` does. **The harder question to settle first, because the fix depends on it:** is the Pi meant to be continuously deployed from `main`, or to be a release target like the Worker? If continuous deployment is wanted — and it has its merits, since it is how the 30 September fix reached users fast — then the honest change is the opposite one: stop pretending a cut release gates production, say so in `docs/release-smoke-test.md`, and move the test-plan gate to merge time where it would actually bite. What cannot hold is the present state, where the documents describe a gate that the serving path does not have. Worth pairing with a version endpoint served by the app rather than the Worker: `/api/releases/current` is answered by `worker/index.mjs:158` before the origin is consulted, so there is currently **no way to ask what the Pi is running** without signing in — the `0.11.0` record could only state it by quoting a terminal someone pasted into chat.

- [x] **A `.env.*.local` for the wrong environment silently bakes that environment's host into the build, and nothing can see it.** Found 2026-10-01 by Lutan: Google sign-in on `test.lannacare.org` returned him to `http://localhost:3000`. **The chain, proven rather than inferred:** `.env.production.local` existed on the dev machine — generated by `scripts/pi/write-env.mjs` for the *production* environment, header and all, presumably left from the Pi setup — and it sets `NEXT_PUBLIC_SITE_URL=https://lannacare.org`. `next build` is always a production build, so Next loads `.env.production.local` for **every** deploy including `deploy:test`. `NEXT_PUBLIC_*` values are inlined into the compiled output at build time, so the test build carried `https://lannacare.org` in **24 places across 19 files**. On test, `getSiteOrigin()` therefore returned the production host, `signInWithGoogle` sent `redirectTo=https://lannacare.org/auth/callback`, the **dev** Supabase project rejected it as off-allow-list, and Supabase fell back to that project's Site URL — `http://localhost:3000`. Moving the file out of the repo and redeploying fixed it: `strip-baked-env` went from 12 vars to 10, and the inlined host went from 24 occurrences to 0. **Three things made it invisible, which is the real point.** (a) The file is gitignored (`.env.*.local`), so it appears in no diff and no review. (b) `strip-baked-env` is the mechanism that exists to stop dev values shipping, and it **cannot** help here — its own header says "NEXT_PUBLIC_* values are inlined by `next build` separately and don't depend on this file", because it only empties `.open-next/cloudflare/next-env.mjs`. (c) The only visible symptom in the deploy output was the var count going from 10 to 12, which means nothing unless someone knows what it was yesterday. **And it is worse in the other direction than the one we hit.** Here a production host leaked into test, which breaks sign-in loudly. Run `write-env.mjs --env test` on this machine once and the *next production deploy* bakes `https://test.lannacare.org` into production — where `getSiteOrigin()` would then hand the test host to OAuth redirects, `metadataBase`, and anything else that asks for the site origin, on the real site, with no error anywhere. **Two fixes, and the second is the better one:** (a) make `deploy.mjs` refuse when a `.env.*.local` naming a different environment is present, printing the filename — cheap, and it sits beside the check already there that refuses when the Supabase project does not match the target (`appEnvForSupabaseUrl`, which is the same class of mistake caught one layer down); (b) stop relying on env-file precedence at all and have the deploy set `NEXT_PUBLIC_SITE_URL` explicitly for the environment being built, so there is nothing to leak and no file ordering to reason about. (b) also fixes the case where the file is absent: today an absent value falls back to the request host, which is right for the Worker and wrong for the Pi, and that distinction is currently carried by a generated file rather than by the deploy. Either way, also worth asking why `write-env.mjs` — documented as a Pi script — had been run on the dev machine, and whether it should refuse to write outside the Pi.




- [x] **A release's PR list is built from `git log --first-parent`, which cannot see every PR.** Found 2026-09-29 preparing `0.9.1`. #213 (`claude/stock-edit-history`, which brought migration `0112`) reached `main` through a plain `Merge remote-tracking branch 'origin/main'` rather than a merge commit naming the PR, so it does **not** appear in `git log --oneline --first-parent <last-release>..HEAD` — the listing every cut plan and every release record uses to enumerate a release's PRs. It was found only by tracing `0112`'s author commit back to its branch, and the release was nearly recorded as eight PRs rather than nine. **Nothing was lost this time**: #213's test plan existed and its release-notes line was a sound `n/a: a shelter user sees no change; the history it now feeds is not shown anywhere`. The failure mode is what matters — a PR the audit cannot see is a PR whose test plan nobody checks and whose *missing* release note nobody notices. Note which gate this defeats: `docs/release-smoke-test.md`'s pre-deploy item is "Every PR in this release has a completed `docs/test-plans/<feature>.md` — **check this by hand**", explicitly by hand because `test-plan` reports red without blocking a merge. A hand check against an incomplete list passes silently, which is worse than no check, because it produces a tick. **How it happens:** any route by which a PR's commits join `main`'s first-parent line without their own merge commit — a branch that merges `origin/main` into itself and is then fast-forwarded, a squash or rebase merge, or a second branch that carried the first one's commits along with it. So it is not a one-off mistake to be avoided by discipline; it is a property of the merge shape, and three of the four shapes are ones GitHub offers by default. **Fix options:** (a) enumerate from GitHub rather than git — `gh pr list --state merged` filtered to PRs whose merge commit is an ancestor of `HEAD` but not of the previous release's SHA; authoritative, but needs network and `gh` auth; (b) drop `--first-parent` and read every commit in the range, grouping by branch name from the merge subjects; catches more, but lists nothing for a branch whose name is gone; (c) **cross-check against the two artifacts every feature must have** — for each file added under `supabase/migrations/` and each `docs/test-plans/*.md` in the range, assert its introducing PR is in the list. This is the cheap safety net and it would have caught this exact case: `0112` was in the range with no PR in the list; (d) a `scripts/release-prs.mjs <since-sha>` doing (a) with (b) as fallback and (c) as an assertion, printing the list a cut plan pastes and exiting non-zero when they disagree. (c) alone is worth having even without the rest, since it needs no network and no new syntax. Worth doing before the next release rather than after: the by-hand check is the only thing standing between an unverified feature and production, and it has now been shown to be checkable against the wrong list.




- [x] **The photo proxy serves any known Drive file to a signed-out visitor, internal attachments included.** Found 2026-09-25 while closing anon's function EXECUTE (`0082`, see `docs/decisions.md`, "Anon loses the functions"). `/api/photos/<fileId>` asks `is_known_drive_file`, which says yes for *every* `attachments` row (blood-test and procedure files, not just resident photos), `project_photos`, `maintenance_photos`, the site photos and Shelter Friend logos, and then streams the bytes with no session check. The only barrier is that a Drive file id is hard to guess; anon cannot list them, but an id that leaks (a shared link, a screenshot of a URL, browser history on a shared shelter PC) opens that file to anyone. And the edge cache (`caches.default`) is keyed by URL alone, so a file a signed-in user viewed is served from cache to anyone with the URL for 24h whatever the database says. Decide what the public side needs: probably the files behind `public_resident_photos`, `public_project_photos`, `site_content(_photos)` and `public_shelter_friends` logos. Then either split the check (`is_public_drive_file` for anon, the current one for signed-in users) or require a session for anything else, and make the cache key or `Cache-Control` distinguish the two (`private` for non-public files). Not a schema-only PR: the route changes with it.
- [x] **Take `is_known_drive_file` back from anon.** Since `claude/photo-proxy-session-check` the photo proxy asks `is_public_drive_file`, and for anything else the caller's own RLS on `attachments`, `project_photos`, `maintenance_photos` and `shelter_friends`; nothing anon-facing calls `is_known_drive_file` any more. `0082` still grants anon EXECUTE on it, and it answers yes for any internal file id, so a signed-out caller can confirm that an internal file exists. A small schema PR: revoke from anon (and probably authenticated: the app no longer calls it), and move it out of `check-public-views.mjs`'s allow-list in the same PR, or that check fails. `check-shelter-friends.mjs` and `check-public-drive-file.mjs` call it as the owner and should be unaffected. **Only after the route change is deployed to production**: until then production's proxy still calls it as anon, and revoking would break every public photo.

- [x] **FOLDED 2026-10-29 (grooming) into *Multi-tenancy build*.** Formerly: **Roles and permissions each shelter configures: only stage 3 (roles a shelter adds at setup) is left, and it goes with multi-tenancy.** **STATUS 2026-10-21:** Done for Lanna. Waits on the multi-tenancy build after go-live. Lutan, 2026-10-03, thinking about multi-tenancy. Shelters are organised differently: one has a staff member who handles purchasing, another leaves that to Management. Today's roles are a fixed enum (`admin`, `management`, `staff`, `vet`, `volunteer`, `public_viewer`) with their rights hard-coded in about a dozen app predicates (`isShelterRole`, `canManage`, `canStocktake`, `canRecordDelivery`, `canArchiveMedical`, `canWriteMaintenance`, `canWriteProjects`, `canDoJob`, `canUseAssistant`, …) and in RLS across roughly 26 migrations. That cannot vary per shelter. **What is wanted:** (1) **A catalogue of activities with no grey areas.** Every action in the system is one named activity, each set per role to **Edit / Read / None** (or **Yes / No** where reading makes no sense, e.g. "record a death"). Where one screen hides two different powers (create vs delete, record vs approve, see a contact's name vs their phone), split it into two activities rather than adding levels, so every cell means exactly one thing. (2) **A matrix in Settings:** activities down the side, the shelter's roles across the top, admin-editable. (3) **Roles defined per shelter at setup:** a shelter can add a role ("Purchasing", "Senior Staff", "Kennel lead") and set its column, or keep the defaults. **Design points to settle in the paper:** (a) **Defaults reproduce today exactly.** Ship the six current roles as the starting template, filled in so that switching to the matrix changes nothing for Lanna, proved by a check that compares each default cell with today's behaviour. (b) **Some things are not configurable.** Admin always has everything and cannot be edited away; no change may leave a shelter with no one able to edit the matrix; Settings → Security keeps its 2-step rule; `public_viewer` and signed-out visitors stay fixed. (c) **Data scope is separate from capability.** A vet seeing only their clinic's residents (0108) is a *scope*, not a cell, so model scopes apart (or as a small fixed set of scope options per role) rather than forcing them into Edit/Read/None. (d) **Enforcement must be in the database, not only the menu.** One SQL function such as `has_permission('stock.delivery', 'edit')` used by every policy and `security definer` guard, and one `can()` in TypeScript replacing the predicates, both reading the same tables. Decide how it stays fast under RLS (a `stable` function over a small cached table, or the role's permissions placed in the JWT by Supabase's custom access token hook, which means a change applies at the next token refresh — say so in the UI). (e) **Everything that keys on a role name today** has to move to activities: the manual's and `/releases`' per-role filtering (`isForRole`, topic `roles`), recurring-job eligibility, the assistant, nav and route guards, the role walkthrough. (f) **Changes are audited** (who changed which cell, when) through `audit_log` (0121), and the matrix can be exported, since it is also what a shelter's acceptance sign-off is checked against. **Define the catalogue once:** the role-by-activity acceptance matrix (Documentation) needs the same list of activities, so it should be generated from this catalogue rather than kept as a second list. **Where it sits:** it is part of the multi-shelter work (the spike just below): `roles` and the matrix are per `shelter_id` once tenancy lands, but the catalogue and enforcement can be built for one shelter first, and it is cheaper before seven shelters' data exists than after. **[STRUCK 2026-10-19: the Senior Staff item is closed — Lutan: *"Senior staff is not a thing … any question about what a role should be able to do is not applicable as it’s configurable in the system."* There is no ordering question left to settle, and nothing here waits on one.]** **What the cards model already settles for Lanna, so this item does not re-ask it:** what a role may do is data today, set by giving the role cards on Settings → Who does what (`0194`). **What is genuinely left to this item is the per-shelter half**: a catalogue and a matrix that *each shelter* configures at setup, keyed on `shelter_id` once tenancy lands — not "what should a role be able to do", which is answered. **Deliverable:** `docs/roles-and-permissions.md` with the full activity catalogue (every page and action, from the manual's topics and the current predicates and policies), the default matrix, the non-configurable rules, the data model (`roles`, `role_permissions`, `user_roles.role_id`, tenancy columns), the enforcement and caching choice and a migration path from the enum. Agree it with Lutan, record it in `docs/decisions/`, then schema PRs and the build in stages: catalogue and enforcement first, behaviour unchanged; then the Settings matrix; then custom roles. **Note 2026-10-09 (`remove-staff-role`):** the default template is now five live roles, not six: Staff is archived (`0173`), so (a)'s "six current roles" reads Admin, Management, Doctor, Volunteer and Public viewer, plus Lanna's configured 2IC, Head of Maintenance and Head of Medical. Nothing else in this item is closed by that. **Note 2026-10-10:** stage 2, the Settings grid, is pulled forward as its own item at the top of Next up (*Settings → Who does what*), at Lutan's request; this item keeps stage 3, roles a shelter adds. **Note 2026-10-11 (`perm-drop-enum`, `0181`):** what this item names as the problem is gone: `user_roles.role`, `legacy_role`, `current_user_role()` and the `app_role` type were dropped, so a role is only ever a row in `roles` and no function, view or line of app code names one as a string. Stage 3 (roles a shelter adds at setup) is the part still open.
  **Status 2026-10-11 (updated by `who-does-what-edit`): stage 2 is built: an Admin edits the matrix on the grid page, behind 2-step, with prerequisite rules and every change in Recent changes. Stage 3 (roles a shelter adds) is not started, so this item stays open. Earlier status: stage 2's screen exists, view only** (`who-does-what-view`): Settings → Who does what shows the matrix, with every box the system does not yet obey marked. Not ticked: editing it is `who-does-what-edit`, and stage 3 (roles a shelter adds) is not started. See the *PRIORITY: Settings → Who does what* item at the top of Next up.

- [x] **Spike: can the app hold several shelters in one database? Measure it, do not estimate it.** **DONE 2026-10-09 (`claude/multi-tenancy-spike`; no schema merged): `docs/decisions/2026-10-09-multi-tenancy-spike.md`.** Measured on dev in a rolled-back harness: one restrictive policy per table holds for all 63 tenant tables, but **all 13 `public_*` views are owner-run and 9 leaked a second shelter to anon**, 17 staff views leaked, and a Lanna admin wrote another shelter's microchip through a definer RPC. Fix tested: re-own the 38 views and 58 definer functions to a role without `BYPASSRLS` → 0 anon leaks, cross-tenant writes refused, no change for Lanna. **Build ≈ 50 h (40–65)**, plus a catalogue lint and a permanent canary diff as the answer to "how would we know". All 10 Cooper `.org` names still free on 2026-10-09; Lutan to choose. Original item: Lutan, 2026-09-28: seven shelters have shown interest — five in Chiang Mai, two elsewhere in Thailand — and the system would be **a gift to all of them**, so the ongoing cost must be as close to zero as possible (Lutan carries his own time and Claude costs, the shelters carry their own domains). **That constraint decides the architecture.** A silo (one Supabase project per shelter) cannot meet it: the free tier allows two projects per organisation and pauses a project after a week idle, so seven shelters means seven paid projects, forever, for a gift. Pooling — one database, a `shelter_id` on every table — keeps the marginal cost of each shelter at zero, because it adds no new services: the same two projects, the same Worker, the same Pi origin, the same weekly backup. **So the decision is effectively made; what is not known is the cost of getting there, and that is what this item buys.** Do it on a throwaway branch and do not merge it: add `shelter_id`, a `current_user_shelter_id()` helper (shaped like `current_user_vet_id()` from `0102`), and tenancy as **restrictive** policies — the pattern `0100` already uses for the `aal2` check on `user_roles`, where an `as restrictive` policy is AND-ed with every existing permissive one. That means roughly **one restrictive policy per table (~45), not a rewrite of all 181**. Then push it through the parts restrictive policies do not save you: **53 `security definer` functions**, which bypass RLS by design and each need their own tenant check, and **58 views**. Report a real number of hours and a list of the places that fought back. **Design the spike around the anonymous tier specifically** — the `public_*` views are served to signed-out visitors, so a tenancy miss there publishes another shelter's animals to the internet. That exact class of miss has already happened twice in this codebase at a smaller scale: `0101` closed the public gallery and the photo proxy and profile photos still leaked through three other views until `0103`, and #182 gated five route trees while a vet could still write the `vets` table through the API until `0105`. **Not before Lanna is live** — go-live is still gated on the Pi origin, the domain cutover and the AppSheet cutover, and one running reference shelter is what turns seven interested into seven committed. But **pre-production is the cheapest this will ever be**: adding a tenant column when one shelter has data is far cheaper than when seven do. Record the outcome in `docs/decisions.md` whichever way it goes. Note what is being given up: one database means one blast radius, so a bad migration takes all seven down at once where a silo could roll shelter by shelter. **The product needs its own name and domain (Lutan, 2026-09-28).** Once more than one shelter uses it, the app is no longer Lanna's, so it should not live on `lannacare.org` — that stays Lanna's public site, and each shelter keeps its own domain for its own public pages. Choose a name for the application itself and register a matching **`.org`** to host the staff app on (e.g. `app.<name>.org`, with the shelters' domains or subdomains pointing at the same Worker). **The whole project is in honour of Cooper, Lutan's dog who died recently**, so the name should carry him — shortlist a few Cooper-based `.org` names, check which are free (Cloudflare Registrar, where `lannacare.org` already is, sells at cost), and let Lutan choose. *Shortlist checked 2026-09-28 against the .org registry (RDAP), all unregistered that day: cooperscare.org, coopercare.org, coopershaven.org, cooperskeeper.org, coopersheart.org, coopersden.org, cooperspaws.org, friendsofcooper.org, cooperslegacy.org, cooperscircle.org. Already taken: coopercares, coopersfriends, coopersrescue, coopersplace, teamcooper. Re-check at checkout; a registry premium price shows only there.* Register it through Cloudflare so DNS, Email Routing and the Worker routes sit alongside the existing domain. Decide the name before the tenancy build, because it goes into the Worker routes, auth redirect URLs (Supabase and Google OAuth), release mail's sender and the manual. **ONE CONCRETE PER-SHELTER FIELD IS ALREADY KNOWN, 2026-10-09: the receipt issuer.** The donation-receipts item hard-codes the foundation's registered address and (later) tax identifiers, on Lutan's decision that a receipt must not read a field management can edit. That is right for one shelter and **breaks outright for several** — a receipt would carry another shelter's registered address, which is a financial document naming the wrong legal entity. When this spike is scoped, the issuer record (name, address lines, registration and tax identifiers, **per country**) is a worked example of per-shelter configuration that is **Admin-only and audited**, not ordinary settings. The receipts build is required to read it through a single accessor so the swap is contained. Related: *Per-shelter Drive* and *Send all auth mail from one sender domain*, which is already blocked on seven shelters not fitting one sender.

(d) **Enforcement must be in the database, not only the menu.** One SQL function such as `has_permission('stock.delivery', 'edit')` used by every policy and `security definer` guard, and one `can()` in TypeScript replacing the predicates, both reading the same tables. Decide how it stays fast under RLS (a `stable` function over a small cached table, or the role's permissions placed in the JWT by Supabase's custom access token hook, which means a change applies at the next token refresh — say so in the UI). (e) **Everything that keys on a role name today** has to move to activities: the manual's and `/releases`' per-role filtering (`isForRole`, topic `roles`), recurring-job eligibility, the assistant, nav and route guards, the role walkthrough. (f) **Changes are audited** (who changed which cell, when) through `audit_log` (0121), and the matrix can be exported, since it is also what a shelter's acceptance sign-off is checked against. **Define the catalogue once:** the role-by-activity acceptance matrix (Documentation) needs the same list of activities, so it should be generated from this catalogue rather than kept as a second list. **Where it sits:** it is part of the multi-shelter work (the spike just below): `roles` and the matrix are per `shelter_id` once tenancy lands, but the catalogue and enforcement can be built for one shelter first, and it is cheaper before seven shelters' data exists than after. **[STRUCK 2026-10-19: the Senior Staff item is closed — Lutan: *"Senior staff is not a thing … any question about what a role should be able to do is not applicable as it’s configurable in the system."* There is no ordering question left to settle, and nothing here waits on one.]** **What the cards model already settles for Lanna, so this item does not re-ask it:** what a role may do is data today, set by giving the role cards on Settings → Who does what (`0194`). **What is genuinely left to this item is the per-shelter half**: a catalogue and a matrix that *each shelter* configures at setup, keyed on `shelter_id` once tenancy lands — not "what should a role be able to do", which is answered. **Deliverable:** `docs/roles-and-permissions.md` with the full activity catalogue (every page and action, from the manual's topics and the current predicates and policies), the default matrix, the non-configurable rules, the data model (`roles`, `role_permissions`, `user_roles.role_id`, tenancy columns), the enforcement and caching choice and a migration path from the enum. Agree it with Lutan, record it in `docs/decisions/`, then schema PRs and the build in stages: catalogue and enforcement first, behaviour unchanged; then the Settings matrix; then custom roles. **Note 2026-10-09 (`remove-staff-role`):** the default template is now five live roles, not six: Staff is archived (`0173`), so (a)'s "six current roles" reads Admin, Management, Doctor, Volunteer and Public viewer, plus Lanna's configured 2IC, Head of Maintenance and Head of Medical. Nothing else in this item is closed by that. **Note 2026-10-10:** stage 2, the Settings grid, is pulled forward as its own item at the top of Next up (*Settings → Who does what*), at Lutan's request; this item keeps stage 3, roles a shelter adds. **Note 2026-10-11 (`perm-drop-enum`, `0181`):** what this item names as the problem is gone: `user_roles.role`, `legacy_role`, `current_user_role()` and the `app_role` type were dropped, so a role is only ever a row in `roles` and no function, view or line of app code names one as a string. Stage 3 (roles a shelter adds at setup) is the part still open.

Ask before the spike reports, so its answer can shape what the spike measures. - [x] **Public website photos load slowly: serve sized copies, cached on the Pi, not the originals.** Lutan, 2026-10-01. **Done 2026-10-01** by `claude/public-photo-sizing` (decisions/2026-10-01-public-photo-sizing.md): widths 160/400/1200, Pi disk cache capped at 1 GiB; the phone-from-Thailand timing is Lutan's. Seen on project pages (`/our-work`, `/our-work/[id]`); **scope is every public-facing image** (Lutan, same day): project cards and galleries, resident photos on `/adopt`, `/adopt/[id]`, `/r/` and the home page cards, pet of the week, the hero and site gallery, recent adoptions, adoption updates shown publicly, and Shelter Friend logos. Staff-only photos inside the app stay as they are for now. **Likely cause, from the code:** every image is the full-size original. `driveImageUrl(fileId)` (`src/lib/google/drive-client.ts`) is just `/api/photos/<fileId>` with no size, the photo route streams Drive's `alt=media` bytes as uploaded, and `next.config.ts` sets `images.unoptimized: true`, so `next/image` does no resizing either. A project card (`ProjectCard.tsx`), the story gallery's main image and **every thumbnail in its strip** (`StoryGallery.tsx` → `ThumbnailStrip`) each download a phone-camera original, often 3–10 MB, so a story with twenty photos can be over 100 MB before anyone taps anything. Every other public image uses the same route, so the same fix covers them all. **Measure first** (a real phone, from Thailand): bytes and time for `/our-work` and one story, cold and warm, so the fix can be shown to work. **Fix:** let the photo route take a width (e.g. `/api/photos/<id>?w=400`, only from a small fixed set such as 160 / 400 / 1200 so the cache cannot be flooded with sizes), served from Drive's own rendition through the existing `drive.downloadThumbnail(fileId, size)` (`src/lib/google/drive.ts`, today used only by the deceased-archive PDF), which also turns phone HEIC into JPEG. Fall back to the original if Drive has no rendition yet. **Keep the sized copies on the Pi (Lutan, 2026-10-01):** now that the Pi serves the site, the route writes each generated size to a disk cache on its SSD (e.g. `<cache dir>/<fileId>/<width>.jpg`) and serves it from there next time, so Drive is asked for a given size once rather than on every edge-cache miss. Small files make the Pi's home upload a non-issue for thumbnails and cards. Rules: Cloudflare's edge cache stays in front (the Pi is the origin, not a replacement); only files `is_public_drive_file` approves are written to disk, so internal attachments never land there; the cache is disposable (no backup, safe to empty, size-capped with oldest-first eviction), and Drive stays the source of truth; when a photo is replaced or deleted in the app, its cached sizes are removed (or the cache key includes something that changes, such as Drive's `modifiedTime`). When the Worker is serving without the Pi (fallback), it skips the disk and goes to Drive as today. Cache each size under its own key with the same public/private rules the route already applies (`is_public_drive_file`, `Cache-Control`). Then give `driveImageUrl` a size argument and use it on every public page listed above: thumbnails ~160, cards ~400, the gallery's main image ~1200 with a `srcset`, and a "view original" only where someone actually wants it. Keep `loading="lazy"` off-screen and `priority` only on the first image. Check the edge and Pi caching still apply per size, and that a staff-only photo is still refused when signed out at every size. **This takes in most of the Pi spike below:** it answers the spike's question (2) and builds its pull-through cache, for sized copies. Afterwards the spike only needs to measure whether full-size originals are worth caching on the Pi too. A releases line (visitors and staff will notice faster pages). No schema.
- [x] **Spike: would serving the published photos from the Pi make them load faster? Measure before building.** **Subsumed 2026-10-01** by the sized-photos item above (sized copies + the Pi disk cache are built; no one should run this spike). Lutan, 2026-09-30, once the Pi was serving the site. Today `/api/photos/<fileId>` (`src/app/api/photos/[fileId]/route.ts`) fetches a public photo from Drive through the authenticated API and caches it 24 hours at Cloudflare's edge and in the browser; only a cold miss costs a Drive round trip. Under `next start` on the Pi there is no edge Cache API (the route feature-detects it), so the Worker's own caching is what covers repeat views. The idea is to hold public photos on the Pi's SSD so a miss never waits on Drive. **Questions the spike answers first:** (1) where the time goes today, on a cold photo and a warm one, from Thailand and from elsewhere: Drive fetch, the tunnel hop, or the image size itself (are photos resized, or served at full upload size?); (2) whether a smaller image or a resized variant fixes most of it without touching hosting. **The caution:** a photo served from the Pi leaves through the home connection's upload, which is likely slower than Cloudflare's edge, so the Pi should be the origin behind the edge cache and never a replacement for it. **If it goes ahead, keep the design small:** a disposable pull-through cache on the SSD (Drive stays the source of truth, nothing is uploaded to the Pi), only for files `is_public_drive_file` approves so internal attachments never land on disk, no backup of it, and safe to empty at any time. It should also fit the per-shelter Drive item above rather than assume one Drive. Success is a measured drop in photo load time on a real phone connection, not a Drive request count.
- [x] **Dates in US order (MM/DD/YYYY): sweep every form and page so a date always reads day first.** Lutan, 2026-10-08: some dates show as MM/DD/YY; his example is the **date of death on the Record death form** (`residents/[id]/deceased/RecordDeathForm.tsx` ~line 83, a plain `type="date"` box), which fits the cause below exactly. **Where they almost certainly come from (found 2026-10-08, check first):** not the app's own text. Every date the app *writes* goes through `formatDate` / `formatDateTime` in `src/lib/format.ts`, which builds "20 Sep 2026" (Thai "20 ก.ย. 2569") by hand, with no browser locale involved, so it can never come out month-first. The month-first ones are the **browser's own date boxes**: `<input type="date">` and `type="datetime-local"`, in **28 files** (every medical form, intake, edit resident, move, rehome, hospital, deceased, deliveries, diets, weight, recurring jobs, recent changes, impact baselines, `OptionalDateInput`, `MicrochipFields`, `PhotoUploader`, `ForecastWindowPicker`, the assistant's cards). A browser draws those in **its own language setting**, not the page's, so a Chrome or Windows set to English (United States) shows mm/dd/yyyy whatever the app says; `lang="en-GB"` on the input does not change it in Chrome. That is also why it is only "some" dates: the forms, not the pages. **Step 1, confirm:** screenshot each place Lutan saw it, and check the browser's language on the shelter's devices (Chrome → Settings → Languages; set to English (United Kingdom) and the boxes turn day-first immediately). If that is the whole cause, the cheapest fix is a device setting and a line in the manual, at no code cost. **Step 2, if it must not depend on the device:** replace the native box with one shared `DateInput` component (and a `DateTimeInput`) that shows and accepts DD/MM/YYYY, still submits ISO `YYYY-MM-DD` (so no server action, schema or `format.ts` caller changes), keeps a calendar picker, works with a phone's keyboard, and decides what Thai shows (Buddhist Era like the display dates, per the 2026-09-20 rule, or Gregorian like the native box today; `format.ts` says the inputs "stay Gregorian", so changing that is a decision, recorded in `docs/decisions/`). Then move all 28 files onto it and add a check (lint rule or `grep` in `gates.mjs`) that fails on a new `type="date"`, so it cannot creep back. **Step 3, the rest of the sweep:** grep for any date reaching the screen without `formatDate` — raw `YYYY-MM-DD` strings, `toLocaleDateString`, `Intl.DateTimeFormat` (`admin/website/PagesAccordion.tsx`, `adopt/page.tsx`, both pinned to en-GB/th-TH, fine but check), CSV/PDF exports (`src/lib/archive/*` uses en-GB) — and the assistant's replies. **Ask Lutan before changing displayed dates:** they read "20 Sep 2026", which is day-first and cannot be misread; switching them to "20/09/2026" is a separate choice, not a fix. Manual note on date entry; `releases.ts` line. **ONE DELIBERATE EXCEPTION, added 2026-10-09: the US donation receipt.** The donation-receipts item gained a **country option** (Thai receipt or US receipt), on Lutans answer that most donors are in the US and US tax status is being sought. A US receipt conventionally carries a **month-first** date, so that is the one place in this app where `mm/dd/yyyy` is correct and **this sweep must leave it alone**. It is not a counter-example to the rule: the rule is about the browsers native date boxes showing month-first to staff typing a date, and this is a generated PDF reading a country field. Noted here because a sweep grepping for date formatting would otherwise find it and helpfully break it. **Done 2026-10-13 (option B, Lutan):** `DateInput` / `DateTimeInput` (`src/components/DateInput.tsx`) now back all 39 native boxes in 33 files, and `scripts/check-no-native-date-input.mjs` (in lint) fails on a new one; Thai inputs stay Gregorian; see `docs/decisions/2026-10-13-date-input.md`. **Step 3 (raw `YYYY-MM-DD` strings reaching the screen) was not swept** — `format.ts` and the en-GB/th-TH formatters were read and are day-first; a grep for undisplayed raw ISO is still open as a follow-up.

Found live on 2026-10-02: the Pi went off the network mid-release and **nobody could sign in or save anything on production**, while every public page still rendered. Three paths confirmed it was the Pi and not name resolution — mDNS (`lanna-pi.local`, `lanna-pi`) silent, the cached LAN address `192.168.68.102` (a Raspberry Pi Foundation MAC) answering neither ping nor port 22, and `POST https://lannacare.org/login` returning `503 x-lanna-served-by: pi-timeout` while `GET` returned 200. The Supabase auth config was checked and was correct, so this was not an auth fault: **"Continue with Google" is a server action, so a POST** — the flow dies before the redirect to Google is issued and the user sees a bare `503` body ("The shelter's server did not answer in time"), which reads as a dead page. Email-and-password sign-in fails identically. **Since this release, test is on the same Pi** (`test-pi.lannacare.org`, same box, same tunnel), so one machine going down now takes writes out on **production and test at once — including the environment you would use to verify a fix.** The cloudflared config anticipates this (`# A second Pi later: run cloudflared there with this same tunnel's credentials and Cloudflare balances between the two`), but there is one Pi. **Three separable pieces, smallest first.** (a) **Distinguish a connect-time failure from an in-flight one in `worker/origin.mjs`.** It splits on method alone — `const idempotent = IDEMPOTENT_METHODS.has(request.method)` — and every failure path returns `idempotent ? null : writeUnanswered()`, so a write is refused whether the Pi timed out mid-request or the fetch never left the Worker. **Keep the refusal where it is right:** a 502/504 can be cloudflared losing the origin *after* the Pi has acted, and replaying would record a second intake (#250, and that file's own comment). But a connection refused or a DNS failure means the request provably never arrived, so replaying locally cannot duplicate anything. Today's outage was entirely the second kind, and **one condition would have meant no outage at all** — writes would have fallen through to the Worker exactly as reads did. Check what the Workers runtime actually surfaces for a connect failure versus a timeout before relying on the distinction; if `fetch` throws indistinguishably, a short pre-flight (a `HEAD` with a one-second timeout, or the status the `scheduled` handler already collects) is the fallback plan. (b) **Nothing said the Pi was down.** It was found because a person could not sign in. Settings → System status has a Pi tile — behind a login that stops working when the Pi does, so the one place that would say so is unreachable exactly when it matters. The Worker stays up in that state and already runs a cron every fifteen minutes (`wrangler.jsonc`, status alerts), so it is the natural place to notice and send the mail `0098` built. (c) **The weekly backup runs on the Pi**, so a Pi down over a Sunday means no backup that week, silently — a larger exposure than the outage. Either run it somewhere that is not the same single point of failure, or alert when a run is missed. **SUPERSEDED 2026-10-26: decided yes and built, see STATUS above.** **Also worth deciding, separately:** whether emptying `ORIGIN_HOST` should be a documented emergency lever. Setting it to `""` in an environment's block and deploying makes the Worker serve everything including writes, restoring sign-in within a deploy, at the cost of the CPU limits the Pi was adopted to avoid (`Error 1102`). It worked that way until 2026-09-30 and is currently folklore rather than a runbook step. **Status 2026-10-02: (a) is done** (`claude/origin-write-fallback`; docs/decisions/2026-10-02-origin-write-fallback.md). A thrown fetch turned out not to distinguish the two cases — workerd words a refused connect and a connection dropped after the write arrived identically — so the split is on the edge's status instead: a write is rendered by the Worker on a **530** (no tunnel connector, error 1033) and refused as before on everything else. **Status, `claude/pi-down-alert`: (b) is done** — the alert run now treats a dead Pi as red (the tile stays amber), so the existing two-consecutive-runs mail and recovery mail fire for it, with what to check in the body (docs/decisions/2026-10-02-pi-down-alert.md). **Still open: (c) (the existing backup tile alerts only after two missed Sundays; one constant changes that), the `ORIGIN_HOST` lever, and the drill that proves (a) on the real tunnel** (stop `cloudflared` on the Pi, sign in). **Staleness sweep 2026-10-14:** part (c) is closed: #567 (`cae7aba1`) made the backup daily and the tile amber at 2 days, red at 3, so "alerts only after two missed Sundays" no longer holds. Nothing left to decide.** **UPDATED 2026-10-30 (Lutan, in chat):** *"I actually have the specs for the item that we will buy, just awaiting a sale on lazada to get best price"*. So the purchase is timed on price alone; do not re-ask the switch-over question below or list it as open. Which unit was chosen is not recorded here. **Formerly titled:** *buyable now — every number it was waiting on is answered*. **This is option 3 of `docs/pi-failover.md` and it is deliberately its own item: option 1 (idempotent saves) makes a failed save safe to retry, it does NOT keep the Pi answering**, so this is not superseded by the failover programme and does not wait for it. **THE TWO FACTS THAT WERE MISSING ARE NOW ANSWERED. Lutan, 2026-10-26, asked directly:** *"Outages are only ever once every 6 months and last no longer than 2 hours"* — so the target is **2 hours of runtime, needed about twice a year**. The paper had listed *"How long past power cuts in Suphan Buri lasted"* as unknown and nobody had asked him. **THE KIT, in his words the same day:** *"the pi5, the wan router, the deco x20, the fr205 vpn switch and an unmanaged 8 port Poe switch"*, and, asked whether the PoE switch had to be covered: *"I could bypass the switch if need be"*. **SO THE PROTECTED SET IS FOUR DEVICES — Pi 5, WAN router, Deco X20, FR205 — AND THE PoE SWITCH IS DELIBERATELY LEFT OUT.** That is the decision that makes this cheap: a PoE switch's own draw is small but whatever it feeds (cameras, access points) can be several times the rest of the kit put together, and **none of it is needed for the app to stay up**. The tunnel needs the Pi, its network path and the WAN, nothing else. **SIZING, worked 2026-10-26 (estimates from device classes, NOT measured — see the first task below):** Pi 5 with NVMe ~15 W under load, WAN router ~10 W, Deco X20 ~7 W, FR205 ~7 W = **about 40 W, call it 50 W with margin**. **THE THING THAT DECIDES RUNTIME IS BATTERY WATT-HOURS, NOT THE VA RATING**, and at 40 W any of these units is loaded at a few percent, so the VA headroom is irrelevant — what is being bought is battery. **A 1000 VA unit is typically ONE 12 V 9 Ah battery (~108 Wh), which at this load gives roughly 1.5 hours: SHORT OF THE TWO HOURS NEEDED.** A 1500 VA unit is typically **two** (~216 Wh) and gives roughly **2.5 to 3 hours**, which is the right side of the target. **So 1500 VA is the floor, and the spec to check on any listing is HOW MANY BATTERIES AND WHAT Ah, not the VA number** — some 1500 VA models ship a single battery and would miss the target. **Do:** (1) **measure the real draw first** with a plug-in power meter (a few hundred baht on Lazada) rather than trusting the estimates above — it is the one number the whole purchase turns on and it costs an evening; (2) buy a **line-interactive** unit (Thai mains sags as well as fails) **with a USB data port**; (3) wire only the four protected devices to the battery outlets, PoE switch on the bypass/surge side or straight to the wall; (4) **put `apcupsd` or NUT on the Pi over that USB port** and feed battery state into Settings → System status, then a clean shutdown on low battery. **(4) IS NOT OPTIONAL AND IS THE WHOLE POINT OF THE USB PORT.** A UPS used twice a year is the textbook silent failure: a lead-acid battery sitting on float dies in two or three years **and the first anyone knows is the outage it was bought for**, which is exactly the class of fault this project holds releases over. With the Pi reading the UPS, a dead battery becomes a tile and a mail through the alert path `0098` already built, the same way the Pi-down alert works. **Also worth pricing: a LiFePO4 power station with true UPS pass-through** (~250-300 Wh, e.g. EcoFlow River 2 class). Dearer up front, but lithium takes thousands of cycles instead of a few hundred, so it does not quietly rot between the two outages a year it exists for — weigh that against replacing a lead-acid battery every ~3 years, which is a small recurring cost and the only ongoing cost in this item. **Indicative Thai prices, 2026-10-26, NOT Lazada and to be checked before ordering:** Syndome ATOM 1500-LCD (1500 VA / 900 W, line-interactive, 2-year warranty) listed between about 5,100 and 6,900 THB across Thai retailers, some before 7% VAT; APC Easy UPS BV1000I-MST (1000 VA / 600 W) cited around 3,260 THB but **it is the 1000 VA class that misses the two-hour target**. **Neither listing confirmed a USB data port, so confirm that on the actual listing before ordering** — without it, step (4) cannot be done and the silent-failure risk stays open. **Done when** the four devices ride out a deliberate 2-hour mains-off test with the app reachable throughout, and System status shows battery state and warns when the battery is failing. **This test is also one of the cases `docs/pi-failover.md` wants measured**, so run it with that paper's timer and record the numbers there too. **LUTAN PUT TWO LAZADA LISTINGS UP 2026-10-26 (FlashFish official store) AND THEY CHANGE THE SHAPE OF THE CHOICE: LiFePO4 POWER STATIONS, NOT A UPS.** **E106B** — 600 W pure sine wave AC, advertised **120000 mAh**, **฿7,760** (from a crossed-out ฿19,999, so treat the discount as theatre). **E103** — 300 W / 600 W peak, **56000 mAh**, **179.2 Wh**, LiFePO4, 3 kg, 3000+ cycles. **THE CAPACITY CLAIMS ARE HONEST, CHECKED RATHER THAN ASSUMED:** mAh is quoted at LiFePO4 **cell** voltage (3.2 V), and it reconciles exactly — 120000 mAh x 3.2 V = **384 Wh**, which is what FlashFish's own EU site states for the E106B; 56000 mAh x 3.2 V = **179.2 Wh**, exactly as the E103 listing says. So no inflation. **RUNTIME AT THE 40 W PROTECTED LOAD: E106B ~6.6 h, E103 ~3.1 h, against the 1500 VA lead-acid UPS's ~3.1 h.** **SO CAPACITY IS NOT THE DECIDING FACTOR AND NEVER WAS** — all three clear the two-hour target, and the **E103 is the cheaper FlashFish and is already enough**; buying the E106B would be paying for hours nobody needs. **WHAT LiFePO4 GENUINELY WINS:** 3000+ cycles and far better calendar life, which attacks the exact risk this item was worried about — a lead-acid battery quietly rotting between the two outages a year it exists for. **THE ONE QUESTION THAT DECIDES IT IS UNANSWERED: DOES IT SWITCH OVER AUTOMATICALLY ON THE AC OUTPUT (UPS / EPS MODE)?** Neither Lazada listing nor FlashFish's own product page says so; one third-party listing mentions pass-through on **DC and USB only**. **A power station without automatic AC switchover is USELESS FOR THIS JOB**: the Pi would reboot and someone would have to go and plug things in, at night, which is the whole thing being designed out. **Ask the seller in Lazada chat: UPS/EPS mode on AC, and the switchover time in ms.** **THE SECOND COST IS REAL AND PERMANENT: NO DATA PORT.** Its USB ports are power out, not data, so the Pi cannot read battery state — **step (4) above is impossible**, there is no alert when the battery is failing and no clean shutdown. **Fair counterweight, and the reason this is a judgement and not an obvious no:** LiFePO4's long calendar life *reduces* the very risk the monitoring was there to catch, so losing the monitoring costs less here than it would with lead-acid — but it leaves the state unverifiable, so it would need a deliberate twice-yearly test instead, and this project distrusts manual steps for good reason. **BOTH VARIANTS READ "Item chosen is out of stock" on 2026-10-26.** **AND A WARNING ABOUT THE LISTING ITSELF: the Highlights block is labelled "AI-generated content for reference purposes only"**, so nothing in it (the 70-minute charge claim included) is a specification — check the manufacturer's page or the manual. **SO THE DECISION RULE: if the seller confirms AC UPS mode, the E103 is a legitimate buy and the better battery; if not, buy the line-interactive UPS with the USB port.** **PRICE UPDATE 2026-10-26: THE E103 IS IN STOCK AT ฿4,760**, which is **below** the Syndome ATOM 1500-LCD (~฿5,100-5,590). So on the three things that can be compared from the listings it now wins outright: **cheaper, same ~3.1 h runtime at the 40 W load, and LiFePO4 instead of lead-acid** (3000+ cycles, so it will not rot between the two outages a year it exists for). **THE DECIDING QUESTION IS STILL UNANSWERED AND THE ANSWER MAY WELL BE NO.** SUPERSEDED 2026-10-30: Lutan has the specs for the unit he will buy (see the top of this item). The E103 Highlights list seven features and **not one is about what happens when the mains fails** — they are about camping, mini fridges and laptops. **A unit with genuine UPS/EPS pass-through almost always advertises it, because it is the premium feature**, so its absence from a seven-point marketing list is weak evidence of absence, not neutral. **ASK BEFORE BUYING, and ask about DC as well as AC**, because one third-party listing claimed pass-through on **DC and USB only**: if the AC socket does not hold up but the USB-C and DC 5521 outputs do, the Pi (USB-C PD) and the 12 V network kit could run off those instead and the purchase is still rescued — that path needs the voltages and barrel sizes checked per device, so it is a fallback, not the plan.
- [x] **DONE 2026-10-24 (`claude/worktree-tooling-fixes`, decision `2026-10-24-worktree-done-wrong-folder`; `done <folder-name>` now refuses a folder holding another branch and `--force` does not override it; `list` names the working command): `worktree.mjs done <name>` can delete a DIFFERENT worktree than the one you named, because it resolves the folder by name and the branch by branch (small; `scripts/worktree.mjs` only).** Found 2026-10-23 by the planner while clearing leftovers. `cmdDone` builds `branch = claude/<name>`, finds the worktree with `trees.find(t => t.branch === branch)`, then takes `dir = tree?.dir ?? folderFor(trees, name)` — and `folderFor` is purely `Animal_Shelter_<name>`. **When a folder and its branch disagree the two halves point at different things.** Two consequences, the second serious. **(a) Cleanup by the FOLDER name half-works:** `done planner-handover-303` (folder holding `claude/record-0-39-2`) finds no worktree for `claude/planner-handover-303`, so `tree` is undefined, the git-aware dirty check is skipped, the folder is treated as a husk, it refuses and offers `--force` — and `--force` then deletes the folder but **leaves the real branch behind**. The working command is `done <branch name>`, which resolves the folder via the registry and does everything properly. **(b) THE DANGEROUS ONE: `done <orphan branch name>` can target a LIVE worktree.** `claude/auto-tiles-out` was merged with no worktree, but a *different* worktree was sitting in the folder `Animal_Shelter_auto-tiles-out` (it held `claude/record-0-39-5`, the release manager's live branch). `done auto-tiles-out` resolved `dir` to that folder by name, refused because it could not check it for uncommitted work, and **offered `--force`, which would have destroyed a live worktree mid-release while deleting an unrelated branch.** Nothing was lost — the collision was spotted first and the folder was cleared by its own branch name — but the refusal's suggested remedy was the destructive action, which is exactly the shape `done`'s other guards exist to prevent. **Fix:** when the folder found by name is a registered worktree of a DIFFERENT branch, **refuse and say so, and do not let `--force` past it** (the same unoverridable treatment as unpushed commits); and when a name matches no branch but does match a worktree's folder, say *"that folder holds `claude/x` — run `done x`"* rather than treating it as a husk. **Also worth having:** `list` already prints the mismatches under *"Folder name does not match its branch (cleanup by name will miss these)"* — make that line name the command that does work, since "will miss these" understates it. **Why folders and branches diverge at all:** worktrees get reused for later work (a handover folder taking a release branch), which is normal and cheap; it is only `done` that assumes they agree. **SHARPER DETAIL, merged 2026-10-23 from where `script-tooling-fixes` first recorded it (as "(4)" on the dev sign-in item):** the lookup that misses is at **`scripts/worktree.mjs:741`**, and the branch it falls through to prints **`<dir> is not a git repo any more, so its contents cannot be checked for uncommitted work`** plus `(--force to delete it anyway)`. **That message is false on its own terms:** the folder IS a live, valid worktree — `git status -sb` works in it, `git worktree list` lists it, its `.git` file resolves. **Only `tree` is missing, not `isRepo`.** So the message invites a force-delete of a working worktree on a wrong premise, **and `--force` there disables the very uncommitted-work check that would have protected you.** Nothing was lost on 2026-10-23 only because the refusal was read rather than obeyed (`CLAUDE.md`: a tool's suggested remedy is not advice). **And it is not rare: a release makes it happen routinely**, since the record step reuses a leftover worktree and rebranches it — the `0.39.4` handover already warned that folders and branches drift apart. **Fix, stated precisely: separate the two conditions** — report "no worktree registered for that name" when `isRepo` is true and `tree` is null, and keep the genuine not-a-repo message for when `isRepo` is false. Matching on the folder name as well as the branch would avoid the miss entirely.

It was not a fault in the loop: the check is a full matrix of **7 roles x 2 locales x ~119 pages = ~1,666 page views**, plus a `/home` load per combination to harvest each role's nav links and ~34 for the signed-out public pass. That is by design and correct — it measures layout (375 px overflow and the 44 px tap rule), so it is deliberately out of `gates.mjs` and CI (`docs/decisions/2026-10-05-phone-width-check.md`) and belongs in the release smoke test. **The actual fault is that it is silent.** Every result is pushed into an array and `report()` only runs at the end; `--verbose` also only prints at report time. Warnings aside, a full run is near-total silence for the best part of an hour. **What that silence has already cost:** the 2026-10-28 harness sweep recorded it as **no output, 170 s timeout** and filed it with seventeen `ECONNREFUSED` checks as possibly broken, when it was merely long; and on 2026-10-29 a stream ran it for over an hour while, from the outside, a working run and a wedged one looked identical. **Do:** one line per page view as it is measured (role, locale, path, outcome), behind nothing — not `--verbose`, since the whole point is to be visible by default — and a count of how many of how many. Consider also printing the planned total up front, so anyone starting it knows what they have asked for before they wait. **Do not narrow the matrix to make it faster, and do not make it card-shaped:** the roles here sample seven different page sets to measure layout, which `CLAUDE.md` puts outside the card rule ("does it only decide layout or ordering? Then it is not security"), and 40 cards x 2 locales x 119 pages would be **9,500+** page views. The `--roles=`, `--locales=` and `--pages=` flags already exist for a narrowed run and are the right answer when you only need to know the check runs. **Worth checking in the same pass:** a killed run leaves seeded rows named `ZZ Width …` and `phonewidth-…` logins in the **shared** dev database, and `--clean` only sweeps rows over an hour old — so a stream that kills a run and stops leaves them for the next person. **Done when** a run says where it is while it is running, and a reader can tell progress from a hang without looking at the process list. **MEASURED 2026-10-29, same day, after Lutan reported "after 2 hours of running it is stating it got no output".** Three findings, and together they are the whole fault: **(1) a killed run yields nothing at all.** Reporting is end-only, so a run cut short — by a command timeout, a Ctrl-C, anything — leaves not one line, which is indistinguishable from a check that produced no output because it is broken. **(2) A FOREGROUND COMMAND CANNOT LIVE LONG ENOUGH TO EVER SEE OUTPUT.** Timed against a live dev server: `goto` costs **4-6 s per page** because Turbopack compiles each route on first visit, and `settle()` runs twice per page view, so a page view is ~6-8 s. That puts the full matrix at **2.5-3 hours** and even `--roles=admin,volunteer --locales=en` at ~25 minutes, against a **10-minute cap** on a foreground command (2 minutes by default). So every unnarrowed attempt is killed and reports nothing, every time. `networkidle` was suspected and is **not** the cause — it settles in 1-2 s; the cost is route compilation. **This is almost certainly what the 2026-10-28 harness sweep recorded as "no output, 170 s timeout",** so that row was never evidence of a fault, and the same mechanism then cost a stream two hours on 2026-10-29. **(3) `--pages` does not narrow the run as much as it appears.** `onlyPages` filters only the signed-in targets; `publicPass()` always runs over all 16 `PUBLIC_PAGES` plus a resident, a story and the phone-menu check, and there is `--public-only` but **no `--no-public`**. So there is a floor of ~20 page views plus seeding whatever you pass. **What a completed run looks like, for the next person:** `--roles=admin --locales=en --pages=/clinics,/enclosures,/residents,/home --verbose` finished in about **two and a half minutes**. **So add, as well as the per-view line:** a `--no-public` flag, and a note in the header block that an unnarrowed run must be backgrounded with its output redirected, never run in the foreground.
- [ ] **SERVE STAFF FILES FROM THE PI’S LOCAL COPY AS A CACHE, NOT AS THE PRIMARY (Lutan, 2026-10-29): PHOTOS AND VIDEOS DONE (`/api/videos/[fileId]` too, `docs/decisions/2026-10-29-pi-mirror-videos.md`; `/api/photos/[fileId]`, `src/lib/mirror-read.ts`, `docs/decisions/2026-10-29-pi-file-cache.md`); STILL OPEN: documents and attachments (SUPERSEDED 2026-10-29: no route serves them, they open in Drive, so serving them locally is a new-proxy decision filed as its own item), and the phone-over-mobile-data before/after timing (pending: needs the Pi mirror installed and run).** **This is deliberately NOT stage 2 of the Drive-mirror item** (making the USB drive primary, which is still Lutan’s decision after the measurements). Drive stays the source of truth; the Pi’s copy is read when it is there and Drive is used when it is not. **WHY IT IS WORTH DOING, and the evidence is already in the repo.** On 2026-10-01 Lutan reported that public pages loaded slowly; the cause was Drive round trips and the fix that shipped was **a disk cache on the Pi** (`src/lib/photo-cache.ts`, `<PHOTO_CACHE_DIR>/<fileId>/<width>.jpg|png`, off unless `PHOTO_CACHE_DIR` is set, which only the Pi’s service unit does; `docs/decisions/2026-10-01-public-photo-sizing.md`). **So the experiment has in effect already been run, for public photos, and the Pi won.** **The gap: that cache holds PUBLIC files only.** A staff file is served `private, no-store` (`src/app/api/photos/[fileId]/route.ts:230`), so it is **never cached in the browser, never at Cloudflare and never on the Pi’s disk** — every time a staff member opens a resident’s photos on a phone, every file is fetched from Google again through an authenticated API call. **The files the shelter uses all day are on the slowest possible path, and they are the ones a local copy would help most.** **WHAT MAKES THIS CHEAP, measured 2026-10-29 against the stage-1 mirror that merged the same day (#1071):** the mirror writes to `/mnt/lanna-mirror/<shelter>/<Drive path>` and **`<dest>/_mirror/state.json` already maps each Drive file id to `{ path, modifiedTime }`** (`scripts/pi/drive-mirror.mjs:147-155`). The photo route looks files up **by Drive file id**, which is exactly what that index is keyed on. **So the bytes AND the id→path index are already on the Pi’s encrypted drive: this is a read path, not a second copy.** Do not build another cache directory alongside the mirror. **THE SAFETY ARGUMENT CHANGES, AND THIS IS THE PART TO GET RIGHT.** The existing cache’s own comment says it is *“safe only because nothing but a public file is cached”*. That reasoning does not extend, so replace it rather than stretch it: **(a) authorisation is checked on EVERY request, before any disk read** — the disk holds bytes, the database still decides who may see them, and no check may be skipped because the file is local; **(b) the response headers stay exactly as they are** — `private, no-store` for anything not `is_public_drive_file`, so nothing new is cached at Cloudflare or in a browser. The speed comes from not calling Google, not from new caching layers; **(c) it reads only from the LUKS part.** The mirror holds medical history and names carers and adopters. The bootable-clone half is unencrypted on purpose and **must never hold staff files**; **(d) a miss, a missing index, an unmounted drive or a read error costs ONE Drive round trip and never a failed request** — the existing photo cache already behaves that way and is the pattern to copy. **(e) The Worker fallback has no disk**, so when the Pi is down everything must go to Drive exactly as it does today. **This is the whole reason this item is a cache and not stage 2:** it keeps that fallback working, so a dead Pi never means missing files, and nothing has to unlock itself unattended after a power cut. **Do:** read the mirror’s `state.json` by Drive id, serve the local file when its `modifiedTime` matches what the app expects, otherwise fetch from Drive as now. Start with resident photos (the hot path), then documents and attachments. **Done when** a staff photo request is served from the Pi’s local copy when it is present, with authorisation and response headers unchanged, falling back to Drive on any miss — and when the before/after time to open a resident’s photos **on a phone over mobile data** is recorded in the decision file. **Those numbers also feed the Drive-mirror item’s stage 2**, so take them once and record them in both places. Zero cost either way. → *Architecture* **NOTE 2026-10-30: the documents-and-attachments part is CLOSED by PR #1095 (attachments were already on the mirror via `/api/photos`; receipts and the deceased archive now via `/api/documents`). The item stays open ONLY for the phone-over-mobile-data before/after timing, which needs the Pi mirror installed and run.** The SUPERSEDED claim above that no route serves documents was wrong about attachments.

- [x] **A role-by-activity matrix that becomes the acceptance checklist the shelter signs.** [done 2026-10-02 as `claude/acceptance-matrix`: `node scripts/acceptance-matrix.mjs` generates it from the manual, the role walkthrough and the Admin-on-mobile decision (93 rows from 67 topics, 7 role columns, EN/TH × phone/desktop boxes per row, a sheet per role, failures list and sign-off lines) and `npm run lint` fails when a manual topic has no entry; the generated copy is not committed, the signed edition is; see `docs/decisions/2026-10-02-acceptance-matrix.md`. **Not built: the printable A4 PDF with cover page and Thai fonts, and the "agree who tests which role / blocker vs accepted" step before the first run** — follow-up filed on the `backlog` branch.] Lutan, 2026-10-02. **Purpose:** user acceptance testing where every feature is tried by a real user **in the role that uses it**, in **Thai and English**, on **phone and desktop** as each activity is really done, ending in one document the shelter signs to say the system does what they need. **Build it from what already exists, so it stays true as features land:** (a) the manual already lists every activity and which roles it is for (`src/lib/manual/en.ts`: 81 topics, 55 tagged with `roles`, the rest for everyone, read through `isForRole`), so **generate** the matrix from it with a script (e.g. `scripts/acceptance-matrix.mjs`) rather than typing it, and fail loudly when a topic has no matrix entry; (b) the role walkthrough (`docs/role-walkthrough.md`, Passes 0-6) supplies the "must **not** be able to" lines per role, which matter as much as the positive ones; (c) the "Admin on mobile" decision (`docs/decisions/2026-09-24-admin-on-mobile-which-settings-and-management-pages-belong.md`: field-needed / nice-to-have / desktop-only per screen) says which device each activity is meant for. The roles are the app's own: admin, management, staff, vet, volunteer, public viewer, and signed-out visitor for the public site. **Shape of the matrix:** one row per activity (e.g. "register a new resident", "record a vet visit", "count stock", "add a Shelter Friend"), one column per role marked **does** / **must not** / **n/a**, and for each "does" cell the cases to test: **language** (each activity once in the tester's working language, plus a full Thai pass and a full English pass across the whole matrix, so untranslated text and Thai layout problems are caught) and **device** (phone for field activities, desktop for setup and reporting, both where the decision says both). Each case has: what to do, the expected result in plain words, pass / fail, the tester's name and date, and a notes column for what they saw. Keep each case to one line a shelter worker can follow without a developer. **The sign-off document:** printable (a PDF generated from the same source, A4, Thai and English side by side or one edition each; the summary PDF's Thai fonts in `src/lib/archive/fonts/` already cover Thai), with a cover page (system version from `/releases`, environment tested on, dates), one section per role signed by the shelter person who tested it, a list of failures and how each was resolved or accepted, and a final sign-off line for the Director. Version it: a signed edition is kept as `docs/uat/acceptance-<date>.md` plus the PDF, and any later change to a signed activity starts a new edition rather than editing the old one. Distinct from `docs/test-plans/` (per feature, developer-facing) and `docs/release-smoke-test.md` (per release, ten minutes): this is per milestone, shelter-facing, and is what go-live waits on. **Before the first run:** agree with Lutan and the Director who tests which role (the walkthrough's two-account role-switching works for one tester; real UAT wants a real person per role where possible), give each tester an account in that role on the test or UAT site with disposable data, and decide what counts as a blocker versus an accepted issue. Ties in with the Thai edition of the manual (Documentation), since Thai testers will read it, and with the multi-shelter work, where a new shelter would sign the same checklist.

Extrapolated, a full run is **~2.3M tokens, more than two context windows**, so it was not finishable in one session at any effort or on any model. **This is a volume problem, not a model or effort problem, and raising either makes it worse.** **So: plan the remaining passes as FIVE separate streams — Management, Doctor, Volunteer, Public viewer, Signed-out visitor — one role each, each appending its own section to the same report, and do NOT repeat the Admin pass.** The five disposable role logins already exist on dev and are listed in the report, so each stream can sign in immediately. **Already produced, and worth acting on before the real sign-off run:** three *wrong result* defects — a bill turned into a delivery loses its cost and never attaches (F-01), a mistyped diet silently inflates the food forecast, purchasing and cashflow (F-02), a visit left "Scheduled" with a past time saves as Completed (F-03) — and four rows where **the acceptance checklist itself is wrong** (F-04 to F-07: a "Who may write outreach notes" control that does not exist, and rows naming home tiles an admin never sees). Those four would have wasted the Director's and the staff's time on the real run. Accepting these findings as items is the *Review the staff dry-run report and spawn the backlog items you accept* item. **Housekeeping:** the run left a standing admin login on dev, `dryrun-admin-20261018@example.test`, full admin with an approved authenticator app (TOTP secret in that worktree's gitignored `.env.local`) — archive it in Settings → Security once the report is reviewed, and do not lose it when the worktree is cleaned up.

- [x] **Clickable links in the text of the website's pages (e.g. DonorBox on Donate).** Lutan, 2026-10-04. The shelter takes donations through **DonorBox** (donorbox.org) among other methods, and the Donate page's text names the DonorBox address, but it shows as plain text a visitor has to copy into the address bar. On a phone, which is how most visitors arrive, that usually means they don't. **Why it happens:** page bodies typed on Settings → Website are rendered by `SiteBody` (`src/components/SiteBody.tsx`) through `parseBody()` (`src/lib/site/body.ts`), which understands paragraphs, `## ` sub-headings and `- ` bullet lists only. Everything else, a URL included, is printed as text. **Build:** (1) **Bare URLs become links on their own.** Any `https://…` or `www.…` in a body is linked, so what is already typed (the DonorBox address) starts working without anyone re-editing it. Strip trailing punctuation the way a reader expects ("…donorbox.org/lanna." links without the full stop). (2) **Links with words**, so the page can say "Give monthly on DonorBox" rather than show the raw address. Use Markdown's `[Give monthly on DonorBox](https://donorbox.org/…)`, since `parseBody` already borrows Markdown's `## ` and `- `. Also allow an email address (`mailto:`) and a phone number (`tel:`), which are just as useful on a phone. (3) **Safe by construction:** build the link as a React element from the parsed parts, never as HTML from the text; accept only `https:`, `http:`, `mailto:`, `tel:` and paths on this site (`/adopt`, `/friends/join`), and print anything else (`javascript:`, `data:`) as plain text.
